title: Two Choices Instead of One Order
summary:
In the previous lesson you saw that the repeated «no» is part of your child's growing independence. Today, here is a simple tool that may help you: give them some control over small things, with two choices that are both acceptable to you, instead of a question whose answer is yes or no, or a bare order. Instead of «Put on this shirt», say: «Will you wear the blue or the red?» What you want happens either way, but they feel they have a say in it. At meals, do not use two choices as a way to force them to eat: your role is to offer healthy food that suits their age, and theirs is to decide whether to eat it and how much. If they refuse a food, do not force them; offer it again another time. Look at what they eat over a week, not at a single meal; if they are active, gaining weight and seem well, they are getting enough to eat.

Choices have simple rules: both options must really be acceptable to you, so do not offer a choice you will not carry out. They should be small and clear, so they can understand them at their age. And do not offer a choice about anything that touches their safety, such as buckling them into their car seat every time; there you state the rule calmly and carry it out, and you can give them a choice about something else, such as which toy they carry on the way.

Tell them before a change what will happen, then offer the two choices: «We will read a story, then sleep. Which of the two stories do you want?»

If they choose neither, look first: Are they tired, hungry, in pain or ill, or upset about something? If a need shows, meet it. Otherwise, choose calmly yourself: «I will choose the blue today», and carry out what you said without a long discussion, and without shouting or threats. Do not offer them sweets to make them choose; that is a bribe.

When they choose and cooperate, praise them with specific words: «You chose the blue shirt and put it on!» Choices may help them cooperate, but they do not prevent every refusal or tantrum; if a tantrum comes, return to safety and calm first.

Talk with the pediatrician if the tantrums are very frequent or last longer than expected for their age, if they cannot calm down, if they hurt themselves or others, if the tantrums get in the way of daily life, if they lose skills they once had, or if they seem withdrawn, sad, or very demanding and unsatisfied most of the time. If there is a serious injury or you cannot keep them safe, seek urgent help straight away.
try_this: Today: In one situation of your child's day, such as dressing or choosing a story, offer them two choices that are acceptable to you instead of a direct order, and notice how they respond.
reflection_prompts: In which situation did the choices help your child, and what did you do when they chose neither?
